mcqs.question: Compared to a binary search tree, what ordering guarantee does the heap property actually give?
options: Only that a node is ordered relative to its own direct children, with siblings unrelated
A full left-to-right sorted ordering equivalent to a BST's in-order traversal
That every node's left subtree is smaller than its right subtree
That any two nodes at the same depth are ordered relative to each other
mcqs.explanation: The heap property is strictly local: a parent versus its own two children, nothing more. A BST guarantees the full ordering in the other three options; a heap deliberately gives none of that up front because a priority queue only ever needs the current extreme value.

mcqs.question: In a 0-indexed array-backed binary heap, what is the index of the left child of the node at index 4?
mcqs.explanation: leftChild(i) = 2*i + 1, so for i = 4 that's 2*4 + 1 = 9. 8 would be the result of forgetting the +1 offset, a common off-by-one when translating the formula from a 1-indexed layout.

mcqs.question: You print a min-heap's backing array left to right and see [1, 3, 2, 7, 6, 5, 4]. Is this array sorted?
options: Yes, min-heaps always print in ascending order
No — the heap property only constrains each parent against its own children, so siblings and cousins can appear in any order
No, because this array actually violates the min-heap property
Yes, but only because the array happens to have exactly 7 elements
mcqs.explanation: The array is a perfectly valid min-heap (every arr[i] <= its children) but is not sorted — 7 and 6 are siblings with no required relationship to each other. Assuming heap order implies array order is one of the most common heap mistakes.

mcqs.question: Why must a binary heap be a complete tree rather than just any binary tree satisfying the parent/child ordering rule?
options: Completeness is only a performance nicety, not required for correctness
Completeness lets values be stored in any order within a level
Completeness guarantees the tree is height-balanced automatically
Completeness is what makes the array index formulas (2i+1, 2i+2) always land on real nodes, with no gaps to represent
mcqs.explanation: Without completeness the array trick breaks down: index formulas would sometimes point at nonexistent nodes, forcing null markers or pointers. Completeness also bounds the height at floor(log2 n), which is the real reason heap operations are O(log n) — but the array-validity reason is the more fundamental one.

mcqs.question: In a valid min-heap, which relationship is guaranteed to always hold?
options: A node's left child is always less than or equal to its right child
Every node at depth d is smaller than every node at depth d+1
The root is less than or equal to every other node in the heap
Two sibling subtrees are always ordered relative to each other
mcqs.explanation: Root-is-minimum is the one guarantee that propagates transitively down every ancestor chain, so it holds against every other node. Left-vs-right child ordering, cross-level ordering, and sibling-subtree ordering are all unconstrained by the heap property.
